# An `unsafe` setter's obligation lasts as long as its object holds what it stored

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `a3552fb` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/obligation-spans-what-the-holder-keeps`, made on
2026-11-14 at the user's direction after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Safety, its soundness measure.

## Signal

Review findings that recur across batches, in one objective and category (`evolution` §2):
two successive reviews of one module found the same defect in the contract of one `unsafe`
setter, an obligation whose duration ends before what safe code can still do with the value.

## Evidence

- `wave-194/batch-5/run-1`, `contracts/ffi_import/settings-ptr-admits-a-reason-that-dies-first`:
  `ParserMut::set_settings_ptr` asked for a table sound "for as long as the parser executes
  with it", and nothing of a reason its callbacks set, which the safe `ParserRef::reason` reads
  long after; fixed by asking that the reason live "while the parser holds it".
- `wave-194/batch-6/run-1`, `contracts/ffi_import/settings-ptr-bounds-a-table-by-later-safe-calls`:
  the same contract, and `set_data`'s, still bounded the table and the context by when the
  parser "executes", which the safe dispatchers make at any time; a caller who frees the table
  after its last parse reaches a use after free from safe code (ASan); fixed by "for as long as
  the parser holds it: until … replaced … or cleared, or else for as long as the parser lives".

In both, the code was right and the obligation's span was wrong: it was stated over the calls
during which C uses the value, while the safe API, not the `unsafe` caller, decides when those
calls happen.

## Destination

The spec: `binding`'s Safe boundary section, or `binding-symbols`' Globals and Function
pointers, which no reviewer evolves, and `reviewing`'s Contracts objective (§3.2), which this
role evolves, as a case to try.

## Change

Not made. In `binding` § Safe boundary, after the paragraph on `unsafe fn`s:

> The obligation of an `unsafe` function that stores a value its object keeps, a pointer a
> later call follows, lasts for as long as the object holds the value: until a setter replaces
> it or a re-initialiser clears it, naming which, or else for as long as the object lives. It
> is never bounded by the calls that use the value, which safe code makes after the `unsafe`
> call has returned.

In `reviewing` § 3.2, beside the case of an obligation stated on code C calls: "an obligation
whose duration is a span of calls safe code can extend, such as \"while it executes\", rather
than what the object holds".

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| an `unsafe` function that stores a value its object keeps has an obligation lasting as long as the object holds it, never bounded by the calls that use it | `libgit2-crustify`, `obligation-spans-what-the-holder-keeps` | crustify `a3552fb` | an `unsafe` setter's obligation was stated as "while it executes", which safe calls made after it extend: a use-after-free from safe code, twice in one module | a `ub` or `contracts` finding of the `hidden-dependency` pattern on an `unsafe` setter whose contract bounds its obligation by a span of calls | watched |

## Validation

None run: both findings were fixed in place, and each regression test is in `ub_unsafe`.

## Review

None yet.

name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. A rebase of a change to
the text of skills, agents or templates alone, no script or program among its files, is the
exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its
parent as in the reviewed commit and its parent: the review then read the same diff against
the same text. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

  of Crustify;

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)

lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries

entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

## Choosing a borrow

Reached when dropping the Rust value does *not* release the object. When it
does, the answer is an owner — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing).

- **No — C, or a parent object, releases it.** Borrow it:
  - one object → `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`, its lifetime tied to whatever
    keeps it alive (a parent's handle, the call);
  - a run of elements → `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>`;
  - a counted run of immutable bytes an object lends, `const uint8_t *data`
    with its `size_t len` (from a getter pair, or two fields) → `&'a [u8]`
    from `core::slice::from_raw_parts`, tied to the shared handle's `'a`, as a
    NUL string is a `&CStr`. A run of other `CPlainElem` values is the same
    `&'a [T]`. The SAFETY comment shows, from C's contract, that:
    - nothing writes, moves or frees the bytes while the shared handle lives:
      no routine reachable through a `FooRef` writes, grows or reallocates
      them (not one on `FooRef`, not one on a `FooLocked` taken beside it, not
      another thread's, if `Foo` is `Sync`); a write reachable only through
      `FooMut` is excluded by the borrow;
    - they live as long as the object does, freed with it or with a parent the
      lifetime covers, not by the next call that refills a shared buffer; and
    - `data` addresses `len` initialised bytes in one allocation. A NULL or
      empty run returns `&[]` without the call, since `from_raw_parts` takes
      no NULL even for a length of 0.

    Where any of these fails, as for a cache, a buffer the library refills or
    reallocates behind a `const` pointer, or state another thread writes, the
    run is a `CSlice<'a, u8>` built with `CSlice::from_raw_parts`, which forms
    no reference: `elems`, `copy_to_slice` and `to_cvec` copy the bytes out.
    The element type does not decide between the two, since a `u8` is plain
    either way: who may write the bytes does. A caller that keeps the bytes
    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;
  - a NULL-terminated array of pointers → `CNullTerminated<'a, T>`, an
    `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a
    `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe
    getter;
  - an object every access reaches under one lock covering all of it —
    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;
  - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow,
    on the terms of a counted byte run above;
  - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit<T>` from
    `ptr.cast::<MaybeUninit<T>>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type;
decided for the C type, not for `S`; since their methods may call any slot,

threads does. Where the handles stay on their thread, as `define_ctype!`'s
do unless the binding opts in, the binding says so once per type with

releases it through the slot declared `release`. C keeps it past any borrow

as `CPayload::into_raw` asks `Send + Sync`; the `unsafe` `into_c_local` asks
only `'static`, its caller stating the threads C uses. Where the binding has one owner for every table of that
type, C's and Rust's alike (`CBox<WriteStream, WriteStreamFree>`, whose
policy calls the `free` slot), the surrendered pointer is adopted into it with

releases through the `free` slot. ffibox does not add a trait for that
obligation, which is one block per table type.

borrows and keepalive, `&` / `&mut` exclusivity for access, `Send` / `Sync`

and slices for cardinality. A convention that one primitive cannot express is
a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;

    `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a
    `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe
    getter;

    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;

a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

### 3.2 Contracts (`contracts`)

Safety contracts that are incorrect, incomplete or ambiguous:

- the `# Safety` obligation of a public entry point that must legitimately stay unsafe: a
  caller who honours it can still reach undefined behaviour, or it asks for something the
  implementation does not need;
- the `// SAFETY:` justification of an `unsafe` block: the invariant it claims does not
  hold on every path that reaches the block, or no comment justifies the block at all;
- an obligation stated on code that C calls once a value is handed to it, such as the
  members of a callback table a safe constructor builds for C to install: C, not the Rust
  caller, then chooses the arguments, often from data it reads, so no caller can honour it.
  What the obligation excludes is refused in Rust, in front of the C, instead, where Rust
  can test it, such as a value, a range, a null or a length. One Rust cannot test, such as
  a pointer's liveness or family, or a string's terminator, is kept by whoever hands the
  value to C: the C declaration's own contract, which the code it calls trusts as an
  export does, or an `unsafe` installer whose Rust caller vouches for it. Only an
  obligation neither covers, and Rust can test, is a finding.

A contract is tested by trying to break it: an input, a call sequence or an interleaving
that honours the obligation, or reaches the block through safe code, and still violates
what the `unsafe` relies on. Contracts are judged by the side of the boundary they serve:
the gateways through which C reaches the crate, its `ffi_export` regions, and every other
unsafe code, which in a Crustify-generated crate sits in its `ffi_import` regions, whose
items are sound for every input their module can give them, as
[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section requires.

**Verdict: rejected, with one fix required.** The rule is sound for a value only one object holds. It is too narrow where the C copies the stored value somewhere else, and there it contradicts the `soundness` skill's `hidden-dependency` pattern. I changed, committed and landed nothing, and ran no gate or rerun.

## Required fix

**The new paragraph (`skills/rust/binding/SKILL.md:33-37`) contradicts `hidden-dependency` when the C copies the value.** The paragraph says the obligation lasts "as long as the object holds the value", ending when a setter replaces it, a re-initialiser clears it, or the object dies.

`hidden-dependency` bounds a stored pointer "by its longest-lived reader", and one of its own examples is "lent memory the C copied into a second slot". When the C copies a stored pointer into another object, the copy can outlive the original holder. A `dup` routine that copies a handle's stored options is one case. A config struct copied into a sub-object is another, and libgit2 has those.

A binder following the new paragraph would write a contract that lets the caller free the value once the first object drops it. Safe code could then still reach the value through the copy, which is a use-after-free.

The fix can't be made by removing text alone, because the object-bound span is the core of the sentence. The smallest fix is a substitution:
- "a value its object keeps" → "a value C keeps";
- "as long as the object holds the value" → "as long as C holds it, in the object or in any copy C makes of it";
- "as long as the object lives" → "as long as its holders live".

## Checks that passed
- **Evidence:** both cited findings exist under `crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c/wave-194/`. They are in two batches of one module, under the same objective and category (`contracts/ffi_import`). Batch-6 has an ASan use-after-free reproducer, and its fixed wording is the rule's.
- **Goal:** it serves Safety, measured by soundness.
- **Placement:** `binding` is not a protected path, and the paragraph uses none of the target's names. Ports reach it, because `porting` applies `binding`'s Safe boundary section unchanged. Reviewers reach it, because `reviewing` § 3.2 sends them to that section. So leaving out the drafted § 3.2 case loses nothing.
- **Other rules:** it refines `binding-types` § 4's "unsafe setter whose caller contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation" and conflicts with nothing else.
- **`ffibox`:** the paragraph names no primitive. It agrees with `docs/borrows.md` ("live as long as the object does … not by the next call that refills a shared buffer") and with `into_c` in `docs/vtables.md` ("C keeps it past any borrow").
- **Weakens a check:** no.
- **Commit:** one commit, `a3552fb`, directly on `e8e55af`. The author is Marius Momeu with crustify as co-author, which matches the campaign's `identity` answer.
- **Record row:** the recurrence signal is one a campaign would observe, since every `ub` or `contracts` finding names its pattern. `watched` is the right status.
- **Validation:** per your instruction, the batch that met the defect stands as the validation.

## Not required
1. **The proposal's Change section is out of date.** It still says "Not made", quotes an earlier wording, and drafts the § 3.2 case. This can be fixed by removing text: drop "Not made" and the § 3.2 draft, quote the commit's text, and add one line saying why the case was left out.
2. **Batch-5 is only partly answered.** Its reason string was stored by a callback the setter installs, not by the setter itself. `soundness`'s closing rule, that a contract is re-derived from every safe method relying on it, covers that omission. Covering it in this paragraph would mean adding a rule.
3. **Wording:**
   - "an `unsafe` function" sits right after the previous paragraph's "`unsafe fn`", which breaks one term per thing.
   - "re-initialiser" appears nowhere else in the skills.
   - "the contract naming which" could also name the calls that keep the value, as batch-6's `reset` did.
4. **The record row's recurrence signal** could be widened alongside the required fix, to: "bounds its obligation by a span of calls, or by one holder where the C copies the value".
5. **Three evolution branches are stacked on `a3552fb`:** `global-the-program-may-set`, `callback-context-in-an-argument` and `callback-reenters-its-caller`. None of them changes `binding/SKILL.md`, so after the fix they can be rebased under the exception for unchanged diffs without a new review.

I filed no proposal or lesson, and changed nothing in Crustify.
